analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection queues appear in this snapshot — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage projects waiting somewhere between initial study and commissioning as of September 3, 2026. These totals represent planned capacity that has requested a grid connection, not actual data center demand, and the five queues are not directly comparable to one another: each operator defines scope differently, counts withdrawn or completed projects differently, and covers a different geographic footprint. ERCOT's Texas queue alone lists 438,086 MW across 1,778 requests, while CAISO's active California queue is the smallest here at 71,682 MW across 265 requests, reflecting both California's narrower active-only scope and Texas's outsized pipeline of new projects.

For readers focused on AI data centers, the fuel-type breakdown is where the signal lies. Battery storage and natural gas — the two resources most tightly coupled to large, around-the-clock loads — are growing prominently in the queues that cover the states where data center construction is most concentrated. ERCOT shows 159,820 MW of storage and 78,092 MW of gas queued; SPP shows 52,913 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas; MISO shows 68,429 MW of storage and 30,236 MW of gas; and CAISO shows 46,944 MW of storage and 916 MW of gas. Storage at this scale in interconnection queues tends to follow load that needs firm, dispatchable backup or peak-shaving capacity, which is a characteristic signature of large hyperscale campuses, though the queue data alone cannot confirm that relationship.

The EIA commercial electricity sales figures, covering June 2026 for eight states, add a partial demand-side picture: Texas reported 15,754 GWh of commercial-sector sales that month at an average price of $8.66 per MWh, Virginia reported 7,771 GWh at $10.99, and California reported 10,025 GWh at $27.33, though these are commercial-class sales broadly and are a proxy for data center load rather than a direct measurement of it. Prices vary from $8.66 in Texas to $27.33 in California, a spread that helps explain why interconnection queues in lower-cost states remain so large. The most informative next development to watch will be how many of the gas and storage projects in each queue advance from study into signed interconnection agreements over the coming quarterly reporting cycles, since that transition is the clearest leading indicator that load commitments behind those projects are hardening.
